passage:
Monday: At the park, a smiling man held out a toffee. "Come, see my puppies in the car." Omkar ran toward him. Aai caught his hand and walked him straight to the park guard, who went to find the man.
Wednesday: The new school-van helper, Saurabh uncle, had a big moustache and no smile. Omkar hid behind Aai and cried.
Friday: Omkar's shoe fell under the van seat. Saurabh uncle crawled in and found it. "Thank you," Omkar whispered.

qa.q: Who did Aai take Omkar to at the park?
qa.a: She walked him straight to the park guard.

qa.q: Why was Omkar scared of Saurabh uncle but happy to run to the smiling man?
qa.a: The smiling man and the toffee felt nice, so Omkar felt safe, while the big moustache and no smile made him feel frightened, even though Saurabh uncle was the real helper.

qa.q: How could Aai help Omkar with strangers after Monday?
qa.a: She could teach a simple rule: only go with grown-ups Aai or the school says are safe, however nice they seem.

qa.q: How might Saurabh uncle feel when a child hides and cries from him?
qa.a: He might feel a little sad or awkward, and pleased on Friday when Omkar finally whispered thank you.

passage: The fair was so crowded that Shankar lost Papa's hand near the giant wheel. A man with a shiny red balloon bent down and smiled. "Come with me, I'll find your papa." Shankar reached for the balloon. Then a woman in a plain khaki jacket stepped between them. "I'm Devika, from the lost-children desk." Her face was stern. Shankar burst into tears and tried to pull away. Devika knelt and stayed beside him. She called out his name on the loudspeaker, and told the fair police about the balloon man. Papa came running. Shankar still thought the balloon man was nicer.

qa.q: What colour was the balloon the man held?
qa.a: It was a shiny red balloon.

qa.q: Why did Shankar reach for the balloon and cry when Devika came?
qa.a: The shiny balloon and the smile made Shankar feel happy and safe, while Devika's stern face made him feel afraid, so his feelings pointed him the wrong way.

qa.q: What could Papa tell Shankar after the fair?
qa.a: Papa could say that helpers at the desk are safe to go to even if they look serious, and never to go with someone who just offers a treat.

qa.q: How might Devika feel when a lost child cries at her?
qa.a: She might feel sorry he is scared but stay calm, because she knows keeping him with her is what keeps him safe.

grounding: Shows a young child in a crowd trusting a smiling stranger with a balloon and fearing a plain-looking helper because of how each one makes him feel.

passage: In the garden of their Chennai apartment block, Anand found a bush with shiny purple berries. "They look like sweets!" He reached for one. "Don't touch, kanna!" boomed Karthik anna, the night watchman. Anand jumped. Karthik anna was big and never smiled, and Anand always crossed to the other side of the gate. He ran home crying. "He shouted at me, and the berries were so pretty." Amma hugged him. "Anna shouted to keep you safe. Pretty things are not always good to eat. Next time, ask me first." Anand thought about it. He still liked the berries better than Karthik anna.

qa.q: What did Anand find in the garden?
qa.a: A bush with shiny purple berries.

qa.q: Why did Anand think the berries were good and Karthik anna was bad?
qa.a: The berries looked pretty and sweet, so they felt safe, while Karthik anna's loud voice and big, unsmiling face made Anand feel scared.

qa.q: What simple rule did Amma give Anand, and why does it help at his age?
qa.a: Ask Amma first before eating something he finds; it is easy to remember and doesn't rely on how things look.

qa.q: How might Karthik anna see what happened in the garden?
qa.a: He probably felt worried when he saw Anand reaching for the berries, and may not know his loud voice frightens Anand.

grounding: Shows a young child trusting pretty berries because they look sweet and fearing a plain-looking watchman who was actually protecting him.

passage: The power went out at seven, and Hrithik's Hindi test was tomorrow. By the light of Nikita's torch, he flipped open his science notebook instead. "Science is easy," he said. "And useful. Hindi grammar is hard and pointless. When will I ever need sandhi?" His older sister Nikita shone the torch on his report card, stuck on the fridge. "You got nineteen out of twenty in Hindi last term. And fourteen in science." Hrithik frowned. "That was luck." "Was it luck three times?" He didn't answer. Science just felt nicer. It had volcanoes. Nikita pushed the Hindi book toward him. "One page each, then. By torch." Hrithik groaned, but he opened it.

qa.q: What mark did Hrithik get in Hindi last term?
qa.a: Nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik honestly believe science is easier than Hindi?
qa.a: He enjoys science and feels excited by things like volcanoes, and that happy feeling makes it seem easy and useful while the subject he dislikes feels hard.

qa.q: What small step helped Hrithik get past the feeling that night?
qa.a: Nikita showed him his real marks and suggested one page of each subject, which turned the choice into a plan instead of a mood.

qa.q: How does Nikita see Hrithik's claim about Hindi?
qa.a: Nikita sees that his marks say the opposite of his feeling, so she thinks he is judging by what he likes rather than by facts.

grounding: Shows a child whose liking for science makes it seem easy and useful while a disliked subject seems hard and pointless, despite his marks.

passage: On the steps of their Indore school, Chetan waved his drawing book. "Art is the only useful class. Maths is boring and useless. Nobody uses fractions in real life." Ujjwal was sorting paint pots for the class mural. "Okay. We have three pots of blue and eight people want blue. How much does each person get?" Chetan opened his mouth. "Just share it." "How?" "Well, each gets a bit less than half a pot." He stopped. "That's a fraction." Ujjwal grinned. Chetan scowled at the pots. Somehow fractions felt more boring when they were in the maths book, and less boring when they were in paint. "Fine," he said. "But I'm still drawing the tiger."

qa.q: What was Ujjwal sorting on the steps?
qa.a: He was sorting paint pots for the class mural.

qa.q: Why does maths feel useless to Chetan?
qa.a: He loves art and feels bored and grumpy about maths, so his feelings tell him maths is pointless, even though he uses fractions when sharing paint.

qa.q: How could Chetan's maths teacher use what happened on the steps?
qa.a: The teacher could give him problems about paint and drawing, so the subject he dislikes connects to one he enjoys 🙂

qa.q: What would change if Ujjwal had simply argued that maths is important?
qa.a: Chetan would probably have dug in, because an argument would not change his feeling; the paint problem let him discover the use himself.

grounding: Shows a child who likes art finding it useful and easy while a disliked subject, maths, feels boring and pointless.

passage:
"Gurpreet Bua, did you know attacking batsmen score more in the second innings?"
"Attacking?"
"The ones who hit big. I worked it out from the scorecards. Averages are super easy."
"And your history homework?"
"History is pointless. Who cares what happened four hundred years ago?"
Gurpreet Bua put down the peas she was shelling. "Nitin, what are the scorecards from?"
"Old matches."
"From the past?"
"That's different. That's cricket."
"You're telling me you'll look up a match from 1983 for fun but not a battle from 1526."
"The match is interesting. The battle is just dates."
"Hm. The battle had a winner, a loser, and a surprise ending."
Nitin paused. "Did it?"
"Read chapter four and tell me."

qa.q: What was Gurpreet Bua shelling while they talked?
qa.a: She was shelling peas.

qa.q: Why do averages feel easy to Nitin while history feels pointless?
qa.a: Nitin loves cricket and feels excited working out scorecards, so that feels easy and useful, while history bores him and seems pointless.

qa.q: Which part of Gurpreet Bua's approach works, and why?
qa.a: Linking history to what he enjoys, with a winner, a loser and a surprise ending, works because it gives the disliked subject some of the thrill of cricket.

qa.q: What is it like for Gurpreet Bua to hear Nitin call history pointless?
qa.a: She seems amused and patient, noticing the irony that he loves old match records but dismisses other past events.

grounding: Shows a child who likes cricket statistics thinking they are easy and useful while a disliked subject seems pointless.

passage:
Subject: CAMP!!!

Kiran,

You will not believe it. The Class 10 adventure camp in Kolad has a river-rafting day AND a night trek. I'm doing both, obviously. Rafting looks so much fun, I can't see how anything could go wrong in a raft.

But here's the thing. Amma says we're flying to Chennai for your sister's wedding in December, and I've told her I'll take the train instead. Two days on the train. Planes freak me out. Every bump feels like the end.

Amma laughed and said, "You'll go down a flooded river in a rubber boat but you won't sit in an aeroplane?" I said that's totally different. I just can't explain how.

Anyway. Tell me if you want me to bring you a river stone.

Lokesh

qa.q: Where is the Class 10 adventure camp?
qa.a: The camp is in Kolad.

qa.q: Why does rafting feel safe to Lokesh while flying feels dangerous?
qa.a: Rafting feels thrilling and fun, so Lokesh feels it must be low risk, while the bumps on a plane feel frightening, so flying seems risky whatever the facts are.

qa.q: What could Lokesh do before choosing the train?
qa.a: Lokesh could ask a teacher or look up how safety works for both rafting and flying, and compare the facts rather than the feelings.

qa.q: How might Amma see Lokesh's choices?
qa.a: She seems amused and a bit puzzled, since to her it is odd to fear a plane but feel relaxed about a rubber boat on a flooded river.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging an exciting activity as safe and a frightening one as dangerous because of how each feels, not the facts.

passage: Lavanya, you asked for a story for the school magazine about a bad idea. Okay. Saurabh, class eleven, this one's mine. The summer I was fifteen, some boys from my building found an old quarry lake outside town. Green water, cliffs, people jumping. I watched one video and thought, that's the best thing I've ever seen. It didn't even feel risky. It felt like freedom. Meanwhile, I refused to go on the school's supervised swim at the city pool. The pool felt boring, and the lifeguard shouted a lot, so somehow I decided the pool was the dangerous one. My cousin asked me one question: "Who checks how deep the quarry is?" Nobody. No lifeguard, no rope, rocks underneath. I stayed home that Sunday. Still annoyed with her, honestly. But I stayed.

qa.q: What did Saurabh's cousin ask?
qa.a: "Who checks how deep the quarry is?"

qa.q: Why did the quarry lake not feel risky to Saurabh?
qa.a: It looked thrilling and free, so Saurabh felt excited and the danger seemed small, while the boring pool with a shouting lifeguard felt worse even though it was safer.

qa.q: What turned Saurabh's choice around, and what could a teenager learn from it?
qa.a: A plain factual question about depth and lifeguards cut through the excitement; asking who checks the safety is a quick test to use when something feels thrilling.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt when Saurabh stayed annoyed?
qa.a: She might have felt a little hurt but relieved, knowing a moment of annoyance was worth keeping Saurabh away from the quarry.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging a thrilling quarry swim as safe and a supervised pool as risky by feeling, until a factual question intervenes.

passage:
Monday: Tejas watched a video of someone skateboarding down a steep hill road, cars passing, music thumping. "The slope near our colony is exactly like that," he told his sister Ganga. "Easy. I'll do it on Sunday."
Wednesday: The school sports club set up a climbing wall with harnesses and a trained instructor. Tejas took one look at the height and backed away. "Too dangerous."
Friday: Ganga sat him down with a notebook. "Two columns. Hill road: helmet? No. Traffic? Yes. Anyone trained? No. Climbing wall: harness, instructor, soft mat." Tejas stared at the page. "The wall just looks scarier." "And the hill just looks cooler," Ganga said. He was quiet for a long time. On Sunday he skated in the empty school car park instead, with a helmet on.

qa.q: What safety gear was at the school climbing wall?
qa.a: Harnesses, a trained instructor and a soft mat.

qa.q: Why did Tejas call the climbing wall too dangerous but the hill road easy?
qa.a: The hill road felt exciting and cool, so it felt safe, while the height of the wall made him feel scared, so he judged it risky without looking at the facts.

qa.q: What tool did Ganga use, and why did it help?
qa.a: She made two columns listing real safety facts for each option, which let Tejas see the risks separately from his excitement and fear.

qa.q: How might Ganga have felt on Monday when Tejas planned the hill ride?
qa.a: She was probably worried for his safety but chose to help him think it through rather than just forbid it.

grounding: Shows a teenager judging an exciting stunt as low-risk and a scary but safer activity as dangerous, until the facts are laid out.

passage:
Hi Rehana,

I accepted the internship with the design studio in Kolkata today. The other offer was the big consultancy, and on paper it pays more and has a proper training programme. But the moment I walked into the studio, I knew. Plants everywhere, someone playing a guitar in the corner, dogs asleep on beanbags. It just felt right.

Afterwards I started listing reasons for Abba: smaller team means more responsibility, creative work looks good on a CV, closer to the metro. All true, I think.

But here's the funny bit. I only thought of those reasons on the auto ride home. In the studio, I had no reasons at all. Just a warm feeling.

Is that bad? You're the sensible one. Tell me honestly.

Santosh

qa.q: Where is the design studio Santosh chose?

qa.q: What could Santosh do before the next big choice like this?
qa.a: Santosh could write down the gut feeling, then compare both offers on a few things that matter, before deciding which way to go.

qa.q: How might Rehana see Santosh's decision?
qa.a: Rehana might be pleased that Santosh feels at home there, but also curious whether the studio was checked as carefully as the consultancy.

grounding: Shows a student choosing an internship because it just felt right and building the reasons only afterwards.

passage:
First week: At the college film club, Varun heard Pema speak for two minutes about why old films mattered. She laughed easily and remembered everyone's names. Varun thought, she should run this club.
Second week: Nominations opened for club secretary. Varun nominated Pema before anyone else had even stood. His roommate asked why. "She's organised," Varun said, though he hadn't seen her organise anything.
Election day: Someone in the meeting asked what Pema would do with the tiny budget. Pema said she wasn't sure yet. Varun found himself arguing hard for her: "She's creative, she's fair, she's got ideas." He heard his own voice and paused. He had decided in the first two minutes of meeting her, and everything since was defence. He still voted for her. But he also asked her, after, what her first three plans were.

qa.q: What post did Varun nominate Pema for?
qa.a: Club secretary.

qa.q: What did Varun realise when he heard himself arguing for Pema?
qa.a: He felt a little uneasy, noticing that his warm first impression had made the decision and he had been inventing reasons to defend it since.

qa.q: What small step did Varun take after the vote, and why is it useful?
qa.a: He asked Pema for her first three plans, which gives him real information to check his feeling against.

qa.q: What would change if Varun had asked for plans before nominating Pema?
qa.a: He might still support her, but his vote would rest on what she planned to do rather than on a two-minute impression.

grounding: Shows a student backing a person because it felt right from the start and building justifications afterward.

passage: At the hiring panel in the Bengaluru office, Swati watched the last candidate, Samir, answer quietly, with long pauses. Her stomach tightened. Something felt off. Her first instinct was to write "not a fit" and move on. Instead she wrote in her notebook: "Uneasy. Why?" Then she listed what she actually knew. His portfolio was strong. His two references were warm and specific. The pauses came before careful, correct answers. The unease, she realised, was mostly because he didn't smile much, and the last quiet hire had left in a month. That was one person, not Samir. In the panel meeting she said, "My gut was unsure, so I checked. The work is excellent." They made him an offer. At his first review, three months later, his team called him the steadiest person on the floor.

qa.q: What did Swati write first in her notebook?
qa.a: "Uneasy. Why?"

qa.q: Why did Samir's quiet answers make Swati feel uneasy?
qa.a: His pauses and few smiles reminded her of a quiet hire who had left in a month, so she felt uneasy about Samir before looking at his own record.

qa.q: Which step in Swati's approach made the biggest difference?
qa.a: Treating the unease as a question and listing the facts she knew, like the portfolio and references, let her see the feeling came from someone else.

qa.q: How might Samir have fared with a panel that only trusted gut feeling?
qa.a: He might have been turned down for being quiet, even though his work and references were strong and his team later valued him.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful adult noticing her feeling, treating it as information, and checking evidence before a big decision.

passage:
Subject: The flat with the balcony

Gopika!

I found it. The flat in Koramangala with the big balcony and the old tamarind tree right outside. I stood there in the afternoon light and I wanted to sign that minute. My heart was literally racing 🥰

And then I did the thing you taught me. I wrote down "I love this, I feel at home" in my phone. Then under it: "What do I actually know?"

So I checked. Water comes only two days a week, the neighbour said. The landlord wouldn't give a written agreement, only "trust me". And the road floods every monsoon, according to the chai stall.

The feeling was real. It told me what I want: light, a tree, air. It didn't tell me whether this flat could give it.

I said no. I'm sad about the tree. Help me look this weekend?

Madhuri

qa.q: How often does water come to the flat, according to the neighbour?
qa.a: Only two days a week.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri write down the feeling before checking the facts?
qa.a: Madhuri was thrilled and wanted to sign at once, and writing the feeling down let Madhuri respect it while making room to ask what was actually known.

qa.q: What would you advise Madhuri for the weekend search?
qa.a: Use the feeling as a guide to what matters, like light and a tree, and check water, agreement and flooding early for each flat.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel reading this email?
qa.a: Gopika would likely feel proud and a little touched that Madhuri used what Gopika taught, and sympathetic about the lost tree.

grounding: Shows an adult noting a strong feeling about a flat, treating it as information, and checking evidence before committing.

passage: Leela, you're asking because of your own offer, I know. So let me, Sarita, tell you about mine. Two years ago I got the Pune job. The moment I read the email, my whole body said no. My chest went tight. I thought, that's a sign, don't go. But I've learnt my body shouts about anything new. So I did what I always do now: I wrote the feeling down, and then two lists. What supports it, what goes against it. Supporting: I'd be far from Amma, I know nobody there. Against: the work was exactly what I'd trained for, my future boss had answered every question honestly, and two friends already lived in the city. The fear was real. It just wasn't about the job. It was about change. I took it. Some nights are lonely. I don't regret it.

qa.q: Which city was Sarita's job offer in?
qa.a: Pune.

qa.q: Why did Sarita's body seem to say no when the email arrived?
qa.a: Sarita felt scared and tight-chested about something new and far from Amma, and the fear arrived before any thought about the job itself.

qa.q: Which part of Sarita's method could Leela use with the offer Leela is weighing?
qa.a: Leela could write down the feeling, then list what supports and what goes against it, before deciding.

qa.q: How might Amma have been affected by Sarita's decision?
qa.a: Amma might have felt proud but also missed Sarita, since the move put distance between them.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful adult noting a fear as information and weighing evidence for and against before a big decision.

passage: At the playground in Toronto, Bao saw Javier's red dump truck in the sandpit. He wanted it. He grabbed it. Javier held on and yelled, and Bao pushed him right over into the sand. Javier cried. Bao stared at his own hands. The daycare teacher came and knelt between them. "Bao, you wanted the truck. Your hands went fast." Bao nodded, lip wobbling. "Next time, what can your mouth say first?" "My turn?" "Yes." Bao gave the truck back to Javier and patted his arm. A minute later he asked, "My turn?" Javier said, "Soon."

qa.a: It was red.

qa.q: Why did Bao stare at his own hands after pushing Javier?
qa.a: Bao wanted the truck so much that he grabbed and pushed before thinking, and then felt shocked and upset when he saw Javier crying.

qa.q: What did the teacher try, and why does it suit a child Bao's age?
qa.a: The teacher named what happened and gave Bao two simple words to say first, which gives a young child a tiny pause before acting.

qa.q: How might Javier feel when Bao asks for a turn instead of grabbing?
qa.a: Javier might still feel a bit wary after being pushed, but safer and more willing to share when asked kindly.

grounding: Shows a preschooler acting on a first impulse, grabbing and pushing, with little pause, and being helped toward a first small pause.

passage: In the nursery class of the Madurai school, the bell rang for outdoor time. Ramesh shot out of his seat and ran straight through the door, knocking the crayon box off Akash's table. passage: Hafsa, you got the riddle wrong and now you're sulking? Your Rajni Dadi will tell you a secret. When I was ten, in our school in Bareilly, Master-ji wrote on the board: "A farmer had seventeen sheep. All but nine ran away. How many were left?" I jumped up. "Eight!" The whole class laughed, and I went hot all over. The answer was nine. All but nine ran away, so nine stayed. I had heard "seventeen" and "nine" and just subtracted. That evening I was so cross. But next day Master-ji gave another one, and this time I did something new. I put my hands flat on the desk and read it twice in my head before opening my mouth. I got it right. After that, whenever a question felt too easy, I put my hands on the desk.

qa.q: How many sheep did the farmer have at first?
qa.a: Seventeen sheep.

qa.q: Why did "eight" feel so right to young Rajni?

qa.q: What choice did Rajni make the next day, and why did it work?
qa.a: Rajni put her hands flat on the desk and read the riddle twice before answering, which gave her a pause to catch the trick.

qa.q: How might the classmates who laughed have felt the next day?

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a child learning to catch a wrong first answer to a trick question with a brief pause.

passage: The inter-school quiz in Lucknow was down to the last round, and the buzzer was set to five seconds. Farhan's hand hovered. "Which weighs more, a kilo of feathers or a kilo of iron?" Buzz. Next question: "How many months have twenty-eight days?" Farhan's brain yelled "One! February!" His hand jumped. He made himself breathe. February. But also January has twenty-eight days. And March. "All twelve," he said. The quizmaster smiled. "Correct." Farhan let out his breath. The team was still behind by five, but he grinned anyway.

qa.q: How long was the buzzer timer in the last round?

qa.q: Why did "Iron!" feel like the right answer to Farhan?

qa.q: What small step did Tanvir suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Counting one breath before buzzing, which gave Farhan just enough time to notice the trick in the second question.

qa.q: How might Tanvir feel when Farhan gets the months question right?
qa.a: He probably feels proud and pleased that his whispered tip worked, even though the team was still behind.

grounding: Shows a child under time pressure answering a trick question fast and wrong, then using a short pause to catch the next one.

passage: On the terrace of their building in Hyderabad, Afreen was in charge of riddles. "Karthik, a bat and a ball, together, weigh one hundred and ten grams. The bat weighs a hundred grams more than the ball. How much does the ball weigh?" "Ten grams!" said Karthik instantly. Afreen shook her head. "Then the bat would be one-ten and the total would be one-twenty." Karthik groaned. "It sounded so easy." "That's why it's a trick," Afreen said. She gave him another: "If it takes five minutes for five kites to fly up, how long for a hundred kites?" Karthik's mouth opened, then closed. He tapped the railing, counting. "Five minutes," he said slowly. "Each kite takes five minutes, on its own." Afreen clapped. Karthik clapped for himself too.

qa.q: How much did the bat and ball weigh together?
qa.a: One hundred and ten grams.

qa.q: How can you tell Karthik was worried about being caught out a second time?
qa.a: He opened his mouth, then closed it and tapped the railing while counting, showing he felt wary of the easy-feeling answer.

qa.q: What could Karthik do when a riddle next feels too easy?
qa.a: He could check his answer against the question, as Afreen did with the bat and ball, before saying it out loud.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel being the one who asks the riddles?
qa.a: She seems to enjoy it and feels pleased when Karthik slows down and gets the kite riddle right.

grounding: Shows a child learning to catch a wrong quick answer to a trick question by pausing briefly.

passage:
Monday. In the canteen, Yamini's friends were daring each other to sign up for the inter-school rap battle. Everyone was watching. "I'll do it," Yamini said, and wrote her name before anyone else. She had never rapped in her life.
Thursday. Alone at her desk that night, Yamini chose her class eleven subjects. She made a table: what she enjoyed, what the careers needed, what her marks said. She slept on it and asked her cousin Usha, who had done commerce, two questions. She picked economics.
Saturday. Usha took her shopping. A group of Yamini's classmates were there, admiring some glittery shoes. "Buy them!" Yamini reached for her purse, then stopped. "Hang on. I'll decide at home." Her classmates groaned. Usha raised her eyebrows. Yamini shrugged. "Monday I signed up for rap. Still panicking about that."

qa.q: What subject did Yamini pick for class eleven?
qa.a: She picked economics.

qa.q: Why did Yamini sign up for the rap battle so quickly on Monday?
qa.a: With everyone watching and daring each other, she felt excited and bold, so the snap choice felt right in the moment.

qa.q: What lesson from Monday did Yamini use on Saturday?
qa.a: She noticed the friends watching and the rush, paused, and moved the decision home, the calmer setting where she had chosen her subjects well.

qa.q: How might Usha see the difference between Yamini's Thursday and Saturday choices?
qa.a: Usha probably sees that Yamini is careful when calm and alone, and was impressed when Yamini paused even with classmates cheering.

grounding: Shows a teenager switching between snap choices made with friends watching and careful reasoning when calm and alone.

passage: Vasudha, you think I was always this careful? Ask your Deepak mama about the ghat road. I was fifteen, in Kodaikanal, and my friends bet I wouldn't cycle down the ghat without touching the brakes. Six boys, all shouting. I didn't think for one second. I just went. I hit gravel at the second bend and flew into the bushes. Twelve stitches on my knee, and my father's face in the hospital, I still remember it. But here's the other half. That same year I had to choose between science and arts. I sat alone on the roof for three evenings with a notebook. I listed what I loved and what I was good at. I talked to my teacher. I chose arts, against everyone's advice, and it was right. Same boy. Different room. That's what I want you to see.

qa.q: How many stitches did Deepak get on his knee?
qa.a: Twelve stitches.

qa.q: Why did young Deepak not think before cycling down the ghat?
qa.a: With six boys shouting and a bet on, Deepak felt excited and dared, and the pressure of friends watching pushed him into a snap choice.

qa.q: What was different about how Deepak chose between science and arts?
qa.a: Deepak decided alone and calm over three evenings, making lists and talking to a teacher, which let careful reasoning guide him.

qa.q: How might Deepak's father have felt at the hospital?
qa.a: He was likely frightened and shaken seeing his son hurt, and perhaps angry that a bet had led to it.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, a teenager making a snap choice in front of friends and careful choices when calm and alone.

passage: The group project topic had to be submitted in ten minutes, and the whole class was crowding around Rukmini's desk. "Choose, choose," Sharmila chanted. "The volcano one," Rukmini said, just to make the noise stop. Everyone cheered. That evening, alone, she opened the syllabus. The volcano topic needed field data they couldn't get. The water-quality topic could use the tap in the school lab. Her stomach sank. She wrote Sharmila a message: "I picked the volcano to get it over with. I don't think it works. Can we ask Ma'am tomorrow if we can switch?" Sharmila replied: "honestly I just wanted lunch." The next morning, both of them went to their teacher before class. She let them switch.

qa.q: How long did they have to submit the group project topic?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini's stomach sink when she opened the syllabus that evening?
qa.a: Alone and calm, she saw that the volcano topic needed data they couldn't get, and felt worried and regretful that she had picked it only to end the noise.

qa.q: What could Rukmini try the next time a crowd pushes her to decide?
qa.a: She could ask for a minute to check the options, or say she will confirm after class, so the choice isn't made in the loudest moment.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see the snap decision after Rukmini's message?
qa.a: Sharmila admits she was just hungry and not thinking about the topic, so she's relieved to switch.

grounding: Shows a teenager making a snap choice under peer pressure and a better reasoned one when calm, under time pressure.

passage:
Monday. Nilesh took ten seconds to choose his canteen lunch: dosa, like always. He took thirty seconds to reply yes to a friend's movie plan. Familiar things, easy choices.
Wednesday. His senior offered him a spot in a startup: leave college after second year, work full-time. Nilesh felt a rush. He wanted to say yes on the spot. Instead he said, "Give me till Sunday." That night he made a checklist: what he'd lose, what he'd gain, what couldn't be undone. He slept on it. On Thursday he called his older cousin Damini, who had left a job to start a business, and asked her one question: "What would you check that I haven't?"
Sunday. He read his list again with a clear head. He said no to leaving, but offered to intern with the startup over the summer. They said yes.

qa.q: What did Nilesh eat for lunch on Monday?
qa.a: Dosa, like always.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh ask for time instead of saying yes to the startup on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt a strong rush of excitement but knew leaving college would be hard to undo, so he was cautious about trusting the thrill.

qa.q: Which of Nilesh's steps would you copy for a big, new decision?
qa.a: Asking for a few days, making a checklist of what can't be undone, and getting advice from someone who has faced a similar choice.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Nilesh asks her what she would check?
qa.a: Damini would likely feel respected and glad that Nilesh wanted her experience before a big decision.

grounding: Shows a young adult using quick intuition for familiar choices and slowing down with a checklist, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage: Seema, sit. You're choosing between two colleges, and you want me to just tell you? Let your Raghav chacha tell you how I learnt. When I was twenty, in Nagpur, I made every small choice in a snap. Which tea stall, which shirt, which bus. Mostly I was right, because I'd done those things a hundred times. Then an uncle offered me a job in Dubai, leaving right after my exams. I nearly said yes at the dinner table. My mother put her hand on mine and said, "Sleep first." I slept. I wrote a list. I talked to my professor, who had worked abroad. And I saw what I'd missed: my degree wasn't finished, the contract wasn't written, and I didn't know a single person there. I said no. Two years later I went, properly.

qa.q: Who put her hand on Raghav's at the dinner table?
qa.a: His mother.

qa.q: Why did young Raghav nearly say yes to the Dubai job at the table?
qa.a: He felt excited and was used to snap choices that usually worked for small, familiar things, so his quick instinct felt trustworthy there too.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Raghav's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: His mother's "Sleep first" made him slow down, list the facts and ask his professor, which revealed the unfinished degree and missing contract.

qa.q: How might Raghav's mother have felt when he nearly said yes?
qa.a: She was probably worried that a big, new choice was being made in a moment of excitement, and relieved when he agreed to wait.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, trusting quick intuition for everyday choices and slowing down with sleep, lists and advice for a big one.

passage: The storm had knocked out the hostel Wi-Fi, and Uma had until midnight to accept or decline a transfer to the new campus in another city. In the canteen, she picked her snack in two seconds: samosa, obviously. "Just accept the transfer too," said Harsha. "Go with your gut." Uma shook her head. "My gut is great at samosas. This is new, and I can't undo it." She walked to the library, which still had a line, and opened her checklist: courses, hostel, distance from home, what her professors had said. She emailed the office asking if she could reply by Friday, given the outage. They agreed. That night she slept. The next day she called her aunt and a senior who had moved. On Friday she accepted, calmly.

qa.q: What snack did Uma pick in the canteen?
qa.a: A samosa.

qa.q: Why was Uma comfortable choosing the samosa quickly but not the transfer?
qa.a: She felt confident with a familiar, small choice, but felt cautious about a new decision she couldn't undo.

qa.q: What small step helped Uma under the midnight deadline?
qa.a: She asked the office for more time because of the outage, which gave her room to sleep and seek advice.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Uma's refusal to follow her gut?
qa.a: Harsha might find it slow or overcautious at first, not seeing the difference between a snack and a big move.

grounding: Shows a young adult trusting quick intuition for a familiar small choice and slowing down with a checklist, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage: I'm Jyoti, and last quarter I watched our small team in Gurugram get it exactly backwards. Rajni spent forty minutes choosing the font for an internal memo only four people would read. She made a comparison chart. Meanwhile Tushar signed a year-long contract with a new courier firm after one friendly phone call. "Good vibe," he said. I wasn't the manager, just the person sitting between them. So at lunch, I tried something. I drew a quick grid on a napkin: small or big, familiar or new. "Memo font: small, familiar. Two minutes, max." Rajni laughed, relieved. "Courier contract: big, new, hard to undo." Tushar went quiet. "Want to look at it together tomorrow?" I asked. He did. We found a cancellation fee he'd missed. Rajni now sends memos in whatever font opens first.

qa.q: How long did Rajni spend choosing the memo font?
qa.a: Forty minutes.

qa.q: Why might Jyoti have felt uneasy sitting between Rajni and Tushar?
qa.a: Jyoti felt concerned watching one colleague waste effort on a tiny choice while another rushed a big one, but was not the manager and had to find a gentle way to help.

qa.q: What tool did Jyoti use, and why did it help both colleagues?
qa.a: A simple napkin grid of small or big, familiar or new, which showed each person how much thinking their choice deserved.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel when the cancellation fee turned up?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed but also relieved that someone helped him catch it before it cost the team more.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing one person over-analysing a simple choice and another deciding a complex one on gut feeling, and helping both match effort to stakes.

passage:
Team lead's note, Thursday, design team.
Two patterns this sprint. Deepika spent most of Tuesday choosing between two shades of grey for a button, running three polls in the team chat. Kiran, on the other hand, picked a new software vendor for the whole project in one meeting, because the demo "felt solid". I spoke to each of them separately. To Deepika I said, "This button can change next week. Pick one in five minutes and move on." She looked relieved. To Kiran I said, "This vendor will be with us for two years. Let's list three things that could go wrong." Kiran was annoyed at first but made the list, and found the vendor had no support in our time zone. We are now comparing two others. Next sprint I'll put a stakes question at the top of every decision card 👍

qa.q: How many polls did Deepika run about the button?
qa.a: Three polls.

qa.q: Why might Kiran have been annoyed when asked to list what could go wrong?
qa.a: Kiran felt confident because the demo felt solid, so being asked to slow down may have seemed like doubt about a choice that already felt right.

qa.q: What change does the note-writer plan for the next sprint, and why might it help?
qa.a: Putting a stakes question at the top of every decision card, so each person matches their effort to how big and reversible the choice is.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel after being told to pick a shade in five minutes?
qa.a: She looked relieved, likely glad to be freed from agonising over a small, changeable choice.

grounding: Shows a team lead noticing one colleague over-analysing a small choice and another gut-deciding a big one, and helping each match effort to stakes.

passage:
Dear diary, Mehak here, and today was a study in opposites.

At lunch, Preeti took twenty minutes to order. She read the whole menu twice, asked about the paneer, changed her mind, and ended up with dal like always. We were late back.

At three, Nakul approved moving all our customer files to a new server over the weekend. No test run. He said, "I've got a good feeling." I actually felt my stomach drop.

So I spoke up. Gently. "Nakul, could we test with ten files first?" He sighed but agreed. The test failed. Half the files wouldn't open.

And to Preeti, walking back, I said: "Next time, dal. Just order the dal." She laughed.

I think what I actually want to say to both of them is: match the effort to what could go wrong.

qa.q: What did Preeti end up ordering at lunch?
qa.a: Dal, like always.

qa.q: What made Mehak speak up about the server move?
qa.a: Mehak felt alarmed, with a stomach drop, because moving all the customer files with no test run on a gut feeling risked a big, hard-to-fix problem.

qa.q: How did Mehak help Nakul without taking over, and why did it work?
qa.a: By suggesting a small test with ten files, which let the facts show the risk rather than arguing with Nakul's good feeling.

qa.q: How might Preeti see the joke about just ordering the dal?
qa.a: Preeti seems to take it well and laugh, perhaps seeing that her lunch choice didn't need twenty minutes.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing one person over-deciding a simple choice and another gut-deciding a complex one, and nudging each toward matching effort to stakes.
